The process stops at the (random) time when Gt is triangle free. A major question raised already by Bollobás and Erdős in 1990 was what the number of edges of the final graph Gt is. This has been a subject of a long line of research, culminating in [3] which establishes that e⁡(Gt)=n3/2+o⁡(1). General H-removal processes were studied much less, mostly motivated by extending the setting of the Erdős–Hanani conjecture resolved in [25], see e.g. [22, 26]. A process which looks like a dual process in many aspects is the following one, called the H-free process. Let H be a fixed graph. We start with the edgeless graph G0. In each step t we select, uniformly at random, a non-edge whose addition to Gt−1 does not create a copy of H, and turn it into an edge. Hence, when the process stops, Gt is a maximal H-free graph. The case H=K3 is now well understood due to analyses by Bohman and Keevash [5] and Fiz Pontiveros, Griffiths, and Morris [10]. In particular, these results imply the currently best known lower bound for the off-diagonal Ramsey number R⁡(3,k). Among the numerous further papers studying the triangle-free process and other H-free processes, let us highlight [21, 4, 28]. The last class of processes we mention before turning to the main subject of this paper are the Achlioptas processes, introduced in [1]. We start with the edgeless graph on [n]. In each step we select k=2 random non-edges (natural generalizations for larger k exist) f1=x1​y1 and f2=x2​y2. Then, we choose one of them to add into the graph according to a predetermined rule. For example, the so-called ‘product rule’ selects the non-edge fi which minimizes the product of the sizes of the connected components to which xi and yi belong. Indeed, the motivation behind many Achlioptas rules was to alter the time of the emergence of the giant component. See, e.g. [23, 24], for more on Achlioptas processes.
Let us note that an obvious generalization of the processes above would be to start them from graphs other than the complete or the edgeless one. It seems that the reason such generalizations were not studied was that it was not clear what the observed features should be.
1.2. Flip processes, basics
In [12], the following general class of random graph processes was introduced. Let k∈ℕ be given and let ℋk be the set of all graphs on the vertex set [k]. Let ℛ∈[0,1]ℋk×ℋk be a matrix which is stochastic, that is, for every F∈ℋk we have
∑H∈ℋkℛF,H=1. We call k the order and ℛ the rule of the flip process. Given ℛ, an integer n≥k and an initial graph G0 with vertex set [n], the corresponding flip process proceeds as follows. For each t∈ℕ, we sample uniformly at random an ordered tuple 𝐯=(v1,⋯,vk) of distinct vertices in [n]. Let F∈ℋk be the drawn graph, that is, the graph on [k] such that i​j∈E⁡(F) if and only if vi​vj∈Gt−1. Next, we sample a graph H, which we term the replacement graph, according to the probability distribution (ℛF,H)H and replace Gt−1​[𝐯] by H in the graph Gt−1 to obtain Gt. To be precise, we place a copy of H on 𝐯 so that i​j∈E⁡(H) if and only if vi​vj∈Gt. A flip process is a discrete time Markov process. It is (unlike all the previously mentioned processes) defined for all times.
We observe that the Erdős–Rényi process and the triangle removal process have flip process variants. The Erdős–Rényi flip process starts with an arbitrary graph on n≥2 vertices. In each step, a random pair of vertices is chosen and turned into an edge. If the pair is already an edge then the step is idle. The triangle removal flip process starts with an arbitrary graph on n≥3 vertices. In each step, a random triple of vertices is chosen. If the triple forms a triangle then its three edges are removed. Otherwise, the step is idle. Note that the difference between the original processes and their flip process variants is the idle steps in the latter. 1.4. Flip processes, destinations
For a general rule and a fixed initial graphon W, there are several qualitatively different possible evolutions of the trajectory (Φt​W)t≥0. The simplest one is when W is a fixed point, that is, Φt​W=W for all t∈ℝ. The next simplest is when Φt​W converges as t→∞. Here we choose the weakest sensible notion of convergence, that is, cut norm distance convergence.11
 1
 However, in [12] it is conjectured that this setting actually implies convergence in the L1-norm and possibly even in the L∞-norm. In such a setting we denote the limit by dest⁡(W) and call it the destination of W. There are more complicated types of trajectories. For example, in [12] it was shown that a periodic trajectory exists for a certain rule. Further, when a starting graphon is taken in an proximity of such a periodic trajectory, its trajectory spirals towards the periodic one. However, at this moment we do not see a classification of trajectories beyond convergent/nonconvergent (where the former also contains fixed points).
For a convergent trajectory, it is of interest to investigate the speed of convergence. Bounds which are independent of the starting graphon are particularly interesting. More formally, suppose that ℛ is a rule for which every trajectory converges. We can define for each δ>0 the lower convergence time
τ−​(δ)=sup{inf{T:d□​(ΦT​W,dest⁡(W))<δ}:W∈𝒲0}
and the upper convergence time
τ+​(δ)=sup{sup{T:d□​(ΦT​W,dest⁡(W))≥δ}:W∈𝒲0}.
1.5. Our results
This paper investigates properties of some natural flip processes, with a particular emphasis on the description of their trajectories. Due to the key Theorem 1.1, this provides information about the typical evolution of an n-vertex graph in the next Θ⁡(n2) steps.
Let us briefly and informally introduce these flip processes and highlight the main results we obtain about them. The main results that concern either explicit description of trajectories, destinations, speed of convergence or speed of these flip processes are listed in Table 1. 1.5.1. Ignorant flip processes (Section 4)
Ignorant flip processes are flip processes where the distribution for the replacement graph does not depend on the drawn graph. That is, the rule ℛ satisfies that for any F,F′,H, we have ℛF,H=ℛF′,H. Ignorant flip processes are one of the few examples where we can describe the trajectories explicitly; this gives a complete description of their behaviour. In particular, all the trajectories of an ignorant flip process converge to the same constant graphon whose value is the expected edge density22

1.5.2. Stirring flip processes (Section 5)
While the output distribution in an ignorant flip process does not depend on the drawn graph at all, in a stirring flip process it depends only on a very basic graph parameter — its number of edges. In Section 5 we investigate balanced stirring flip processes, in which the expected number of edges in the replacement graph is equal to the number of edges in the drawn graph. We explicitly describe the trajectories of any balanced stirring flip process. Not surprisingly, the edge density is preserved along each trajectory.
